claim: Childhood adversity is a strong predictor of developing psychopathological conditions.
source: Exposure to childhood adversity - particularly in early life - is a strong predictor for developing somatic, psychological, and psychopathological conditions (Anda et al., 2006; Baldwin et al., 2024; Danese et al., 2007; Danese and Widom, 2023; Felitti, 2002; Gilbert et al., 2009; Green et al., 2010; Heim and Nemeroff, 2002; Hosseini-Kamkar et al., 2023; Klauke et al., 2010; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Moffitt et al., 2007; Samaey et al., 2024; Teicher et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research studies.

claim: Exposure to childhood adversity is associated with substantial individual suffering as well as societal costs.
source: Exposure to childhood adversity - particularly in early life - is a strong predictor for developing somatic, psychological, and psychopathological conditions (Anda et al., 2006; Baldwin et al., 2024; Danese et al., 2007; Danese and Widom, 2023; Felitti, 2002; Gilbert et al., 2009; Green et al., 2010; Heim and Nemeroff, 2002; Hosseini-Kamkar et al., 2023; Klauke et al., 2010; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Moffitt et al., 2007; Samaey et al., 2024; Teicher et al., 2022) and is hence associated with substantial individual suffering as well as societal costs (Hughes et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hughes et al., 2021.

claim: Nearly two-thirds of individuals experience one or more traumatic events prior to their 18th birthday.
source: Exposure to childhood adversity is rather common, with nearly two-thirds of individuals experiencing one or more traumatic events prior to their 18th birthday (McLaughlin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al., 2013.

claim: There is some evidence of a dose-response relationship between childhood adversity exposure and psychopathological outcomes.
source: While not all trauma-exposed individuals develop psychopathological conditions, there is some evidence of a dose-response relationship (Danese et al., 2009; Smith and Pollak, 2021; Young et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Learning mechanisms are key candidates potentially underlying the biological embedding of exposure to childhood adversity and their impact on development and risk for psychopathology.
source: Learning is a core mechanism through which environmental inputs shape emotional and cognitive processes and ultimately behavior. Thus, learning mechanisms are key candidates potentially underlying the biological embedding of exposure to childhood adversity and their impact on development and risk for psychopathology (McLaughlin and Sheridan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McLaughlin and Sheridan, 2016.

claim: Fear conditioning is a prime translational paradigm for testing potentially altered (threat) learning mechanisms following exposure to childhood adversity under laboratory conditions.
source: Fear conditioning is a prime translational paradigm for testing potentially altered (threat) learning mechanisms following exposure to childhood adversity under laboratory conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about fear conditioning as a translational paradigm.

claim: During fear acquisition training, a neutral cue is paired with an aversive event and becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS+) that elicits conditioned responses.
source: During fear acquisition training, a neutral cue is paired with an aversive event such as an electrotactile stimulation or a loud aversive human scream (unconditioned stimulus, US). Through these pairings, an association between both stimuli is formed and the previously neutral cue becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS+) that elicits conditioned responses.
evidence: The claim describes the standard fear conditioning procedure, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: In human differential conditioning experiments, a second neutral cue is never paired with the US and serves as a control or safety stimulus (CS-).
source: In human differential conditioning experiments, typically a second neutral cue is never paired with the US and serves as a control or safety stimulus (i.e. CS-).
evidence: The claim describes standard experimental design in fear conditioning, which is established knowledge.

claim: During fear extinction training, both the CS+ and CS- are presented without the US which leads to a gradual waning of conditioned responding.
source: During a subsequent fear extinction training phase, both the CS+ and the CS- are presented without the US which leads to a gradual waning of conditioned responding.
evidence: The claim describes the standard extinction procedure, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Fear acquisition and extinction are considered as experimental models of the development and exposure-based treatment of anxiety- and stress-related disorders.
source: Fear acquisition as well as extinction are considered as experimental models of the development and exposure-based treatment of anxiety- and stress-related disorders.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus about the translational value of fear conditioning paradigms.

claim: Maintaining the ability to distinguish between signals of danger (CS+) and safety (CS-) under aversive circumstances is crucial for healthy functioning.
source: Accordingly, maintaining the ability to distinguish between signals of danger (i.e. CS+) and safety (i.e. CS-) under aversive circumstances is crucial, as it is assumed to be beneficial for healthy functioning (Hölzel et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hölzel et al., 2016.

claim: The ability to distinguish between signals of danger and safety predicts resilience to life stress.
source: Accordingly, maintaining the ability to distinguish between signals of danger (i.e. CS+) and safety (i.e. CS-) under aversive circumstances is crucial, as it is assumed to be beneficial for healthy functioning (Hölzel et al., 2016) and predicts resilience to life stress (Craske et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Craske et al., 2012.

claim: Reduced discrimination between the CS+ and CS- has been linked to pathological anxiety.
source: while reduced discrimination between the CS+ and the CS- has been linked to pathological anxiety (Duits et al., 2015; Lissek et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duits et al., 2015 and Lissek et al., 2005.

claim: Patients suffering from anxiety- and stress-related disorders show enhanced responding to the safe CS- during fear acquisition.
source: Meta-analyses suggest that patients suffering from anxiety- and stress-related disorders show enhanced responding to the safe CS- during fear acquisition (Duits et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis by Duits et al., 2015.

claim: During extinction, patients exhibit stronger defensive responses to the CS+ and a trend toward increased discrimination between the CS+ and CS- compared to controls.
source: During extinction, patients exhibit stronger defensive responses to the CS+ and a trend toward increased discrimination between the CS+ and CS- compared to controls, which may indicate delayed and/or reduced extinction (Duits et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duits et al., 2015.

claim: Meta-analytic evidence suggests stronger generalization to cues similar to the CS+ in patients and more linear generalization gradients.
source: Furthermore, meta-analytic evidence also suggests stronger generalization to cues similar to the CS+ in patients and more linear generalization gradients (Cooper et al., 2022; Dymond et al., 2015; Fraunfelter et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple meta-analyses.

claim: Exposure to childhood adversity is linked to reduced CS discrimination, driven by blunted responding to the CS+ during experimental phases characterized through the presence of threat.
source: In sharp contrast to these threat learning patterns observed in patient samples, a recent review provided converging evidence that exposure to childhood adversity is linked to reduced CS discrimination, driven by blunted responding to the CS+ during experimental phases characterized through the presence of threat (i.e. acquisition training and generalization, Ruge et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent review by Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: The pattern of reduced CS discrimination driven by blunted CS+ responding was observed in mixed samples (healthy, at risk, patients), in pediatric samples, and in adults exposed to childhood adversity as children.
source: Of note, this pattern was observed in mixed samples (healthy, at risk, patients), in pediatric samples, and in adults exposed to childhood adversity as children.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the review by Ruge et al., 2024 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Recency of exposure or developmental timing may not play a major role in the relationship between childhood adversity and reduced CS discrimination.
source: The latter suggests that recency of exposure or developmental timing may not play a major role, even though there is some evidence pointing towards accelerated pubertal and neural (connectivity) development in exposed children (Machlin et al., 2019; Silvers et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern observed across different samples, with citations providing contrasting evidence.

claim: There is evidence pointing towards accelerated pubertal and neural (connectivity) development in children exposed to adversity.
source: even though there is some evidence pointing towards accelerated pubertal and neural (connectivity) development in exposed children (Machlin et al., 2019; Silvers et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Machlin et al., 2019 and Silvers et al., 2016.

claim: There is no evidence pointing towards differences in extinction learning or generalization gradients between individuals exposed and unexposed to childhood adversity.
source: There is, however, no evidence pointing towards differences in extinction learning or generalization gradients between individuals exposed and unexposed to childhood adversity (for a review, see Ruge et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: Operationalization of exposure to childhood adversity represents a key challenge in the field hampering the interpretation of findings across studies.
source: Ruge et al., 2024 also highlighted operationalization as a key challenge in the field hampering the interpretation of findings across studies and consequently cumulative knowledge generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: Operationalization of exposure to childhood adversity is an ongoing discussion in the field.
source: Operationalization of exposure to childhood adversity, and hence the translation of theoretical accounts of the role of childhood adversity into statistical tests, is an ongoing discussion in the field (McLaughlin et al., 2021; Pollak and Smith, 2021; Smith and Pollak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent publications discussing this issue.

claim: Childhood adversity has historically been conceptualized rather broadly considering different adversity types lumped into a single category.
source: Historically, childhood adversity has been conceptualized rather broadly considering different adversity types lumped into a single category.
evidence: The claim describes historical practice in the field, which is established knowledge.

claim: The cumulative risk approach assumes that any exposure to an adverse event will have similar and additive effects on the individual and its (neuro-biological) development.
source: This follows from the (implicit) assumption that any exposure to an adverse event will have similar and additive effects on the individual and its (neuro-biological) development (Smith and Pollak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith and Pollak, 2021.

claim: Childhood adversity has often been considered as a cumulative measure following the cumulative risk approach.
source: Accordingly, childhood adversity has often been considered as a cumulative measure ('cumulative risk approach;' McLaughlin et al., 2021; Smith and Pollak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McLaughlin et al., 2021 and Smith and Pollak, 2021.

claim: The specificity approach posits that different types of adverse events have a distinct impact on individuals and their (neuro-biological) development through distinct mechanisms.
source: An alternative approach posits that different types of adverse events have a distinct impact on individuals and their (neuro-biological) development through distinct mechanisms ('specificity approach;' McLaughlin et al., 2021; Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014; Smith and Pollak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant publications.

claim: Distinguishing between threat and deprivation exposure represents the prevailing approach in the specificity model.
source: Currently, distinguishing between threat and deprivation exposure represents the prevailing approach (McLaughlin et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al., 2019a.

claim: The dimensional model of adversity and psychopathology (DMAP) formalizes the distinction between threat and deprivation exposure.
source: which has been formalized in the (two-)dimensional model of adversity and psychopathology (DMAP; Machlin et al., 2019; McLaughlin and Sheridan, 2016; McLaughlin et al., 2021; McLaughlin et al., 2014; Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014; McLaughlin et al., 2016; Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to publications describing the DMAP model.

claim: Exposure to threat-related childhood adversity has been suggested to be specifically linked to altered emotional and fear learning.
source: To this end, exposure to threat-related childhood adversity has been suggested to be specifically linked to altered emotional and fear learning (Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014.

claim: There is converging evidence from different fields of research suggesting that the effects of exposure to childhood adversity are cumulative, non-specific, and rather unlikely to be tied to specific types of adverse events.
source: Yet, there is converging evidence from different fields of research suggesting that the effects of exposure to childhood adversity are cumulative, non-specific, and rather unlikely to be tied to specific types of adverse events (Danese et al., 2009; Smith and Pollak, 2021; Young et al., 2019) - with few exceptions (Colich et al., 2020; McLaughlin et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The different theoretical accounts of childhood adversity have not yet been directly compared in a single fear conditioning study.
source: However, the different theoretical accounts have not yet been directly compared in a single fear conditioning study.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: 1402 healthy adults were recruited in the context of a multi-centric study conducted at the Universities of Münster, Würzburg, and Hamburg, Germany.
source: Here, we aim to fill this gap in an extraordinarily large sample of healthy adults (N=1402) recruited in the context of a multi-centric study conducted at the Universities of Münster, Würzburg, and Hamburg, Germany.
evidence: The claim describes the study sample and is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Participants underwent a differential fear conditioning paradigm including a fear acquisition and generalization phase using female faces as CSs and GSs and a female scream as US.
source: Participants underwent a differential fear conditioning paradigm including a fear acquisition and generalization phase using female faces as CSs and GSs and a female scream as US
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Skin conductance responses (SCRs) and different ratings types (arousal, valence, and US contingency) were measured during the fear conditioning paradigm.
source: while we measured skin conductance responses (SCRs) and different ratings types (i.e. arousal, valence, and US contingency).
evidence: The claim describes the outcome measures used in the study.

claim: Three different outcomes were calculated for SCRs and fear ratings: CS discrimination, the linear deviation score (LDS), and general reactivity.
source: For SCRs and fear ratings, we calculated three different outcomes: CS discrimination (i.e. the difference between CS+ and CS- responses), the linear deviation score (LDS) as an index of the linearity of the generalization gradient (Kaczkurkin et al., 2017), and the general reactivity which was defined as the reactivity across all phases
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis approach used in the study.

claim: Individuals were classified as exposed to childhood adversity if at least one CTQ subscale met the published cut-offs for at least moderate exposure.
source: Individuals were classified as exposed to childhood adversity if at least one CTQ subscale met the published cut-offs (Bernstein and Fink, 1998; Häuser et al., 2011) for at least moderate exposure (i.e. emotional abuse ≥ 13, physical abuse ≥ 10, sexual abuse ≥ 8, emotional neglect ≥ 15, physical neglect ≥ 10).
evidence: The claim describes the operationalization of childhood adversity exposure used in the main analyses.

claim: Fear acquisition was successful in SCRs as well as ratings in the full sample.
source: In brief, and as reported previously (Herzog et al., 2021; Schiele et al., 2016a), the fear acquisition was successful in SCRs as well as ratings in the full sample (all p's<0.001; see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results (p-values) and references to previous reports.

claim: During fear generalization, the expected generalization gradient was observed with a gradual increase in SCRs and ratings with increasing similarity to the CS+.
source: During fear generalization, the expected generalization gradient was observed with a gradual increase in SCRs and ratings with increasing similarity to the CS+ (all p's<0.01 except for the comparisons of SCRs to CS- vs. GS4 as well as GS1 vs. GS2 which were non-significant; see Appendix 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results reported in the manuscript.

claim: During both the acquisition training and generalization phase, CS discrimination in SCRs was significantly lower in individuals exposed to childhood adversity as compared to unexposed individuals.
source: During both the acquisition training and generalization phase, CS discrimination in SCRs was significantly lower in individuals exposed to childhood adversity as compared to unexposed individuals (see Table 2 and Figure 1; for trial-by-trial responses, see Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: SCRs to the CS+ during both acquisition training and the generalization phase were significantly lower in exposed as compared to unexposed individuals.
source: SCRs to the CS + during both acquisition training and the generalization phase were significantly lower in exposed as compared to unexposed individuals (acquisition training: t(1400)=2.54, p=0.011, d=0.14; generalization test: t=(194.1)=3.51, p=0.001, explanatory measure of effect size=0.179; see Figure 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results and Figure 2.

claim: SCRs to the CS- did not differ significantly between exposed and unexposed individuals during acquisition training and generalization test.
source: but not for the CS- (acquisition training: t(1400)=0.75, p=0.452, d=0.04; generalization test: t(178.9)=1.63, p=0.104, explanatory measure of effect size=0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results showing non-significant differences.

claim: For ratings, no significant effects of exposure to childhood adversity were observed in CS discrimination.
source: For ratings, no significant effects of exposure to childhood adversity were observed in CS discrimination (see Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 2.

claim: No significant effect of exposure to childhood adversity in either SCRs or ratings was observed for generalization gradients.
source: No significant effect of exposure to childhood adversity in either SCRs or ratings was observed for generalization gradients (see Table 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: General physiological reactivity in SCRs was significantly lower in participants exposed to childhood adversity compared to unexposed participants.
source: In addition, general physiological reactivity in SCRs (i.e. raw amplitudes) was significantly lower in participants exposed to childhood adversity compared to unexposed participants (see Table 2 and Figure 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 2 and Figure 4.

claim: There were no differences between exposed and unexposed groups in general rating response levels.
source: while there were no differences between both groups in general rating response levels (see Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 2.

claim: Linear mixed models including age, sex, school degree, and exposure to childhood adversity as fixed effects and site as random effect yielded comparable results to the main analyses.
source: At the request of a reviewer, we repeated our main analyses by using linear mixed models including age, sex, school degree (i.e. to approximate socioeconomic status, SES), and exposure to childhood adversity as fixed effects as well as site as random effect. These analyses yielded comparable results demonstrating a significant effect of childhood adversity on CS discrimination during acquisition training and the generalization phase as well as on general reactivity, but not on the generalization gradients in SCRs (see Appendix 1—table 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from additional analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: Mixed model analyses did not show any significant effects of childhood adversity on the different types of ratings.
source: Consistent with the results of the main analyses reported in our manuscript, we did not observe any significant effects of childhood adversity on the different types of ratings when using mixed models (see Appendix 1—table 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from mixed model analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: Some of the mixed model analyses showed significantly lower CS discrimination during acquisition training and generalization, and lower general reactivity in males compared to females.
source: Some of the mixed model analyses showed significantly lower CS discrimination during acquisition training and generalization, and lower general reactivity in males compared to females (see Appendix 1—table 2 for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from mixed model analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: The cumulative risk model operationalized through different cut-offs for no, low, moderate, and severe exposure did not yield any significant results for any outcome measure and experimental phase.
source: The cumulative risk model operationalized through the different cut-offs for no, low, moderate, and severe exposure (Bernstein and Fink, 1998) did not yield any significant results for any outcome measure and experimental phase (see Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from exploratory analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: On a descriptive level, exposure to an at least moderate cut-off level may induce behavioral and physiological changes.
source: However, on a descriptive level (see Figure 5), it seems that indeed exposure to an at least moderate cut-off level may induce behavioral and physiological changes (see main analysis, Bernstein and Fink, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on descriptive observations from Figure 5.

claim: A higher number of CTQ subscales exceeding the moderate cut-off predicted lower CS discrimination in SCRs during acquisition training.
source: Cumulative risk operationalized as the number of CTQ subscales exceeding the moderate cut-off (Bernstein and Fink, 1998), however, revealed that a higher number of subscales exceeding the cut-off predicted lower CS discrimination in SCRs (F(1, 1400)=6.86, p=0.009, R2=0.005)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from regression analyses.

claim: A higher number of CTQ subscales exceeding the moderate cut-off predicted lower CS discrimination in contingency ratings during acquisition training.
source: and contingency ratings (F(1, 1400)=4.08, p=0.044, R2=0.003) during acquisition training
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from regression analyses.

claim: The effect of number of subscales exceeding cut-off on CS discrimination in SCRs was driven by significantly lower SCRs to the CS+.
source: This was driven by significantly lower SCRs to the CS+ (F(1, 1400)=5.42, p=0.02, R2=0.004)
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical test results.

claim: No significant effect of exposure to abuse was observed on CS discrimination, the strength of generalization (LDS), or general reactivity in any of the outcome measures and in any experimental phase in the specificity model.
source: More precisely, no significant effect of exposure to abuse was observed on CS discrimination, the strength of generalization (i.e. LDS), or general reactivity in any of the outcome measures and in any experimental phase (see Appendix 1—table 5; Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from exploratory analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: A significant negative association between exposure to neglect and CS discrimination in SCRs was observed during acquisition training in both the specificity and dimensional models.
source: In contrast, a significant negative association between exposure to neglect and CS discrimination in SCRs was observed during acquisition training (specificity model: F(1, 1400)=6.4, p=0.012, R2=0.005; dimensional model: F(3, 1398)=2.91, p=0.234, R2=0.006)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from regression analyses.

claim: The association between neglect and CS discrimination is contrary to the predictions of the dimensional model, which posits a specific role for abuse but not neglect.
source: which is contrary to the predictions of the dimensional model, that posits a specific role for abuse but not neglect (Machlin et al., 2019; McLaughlin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results in relation to theoretical predictions, with citations to the dimensional model.

claim: In both the specificity and dimensional models, effects of neglect on CS discrimination were driven by significantly lower SCRs to the CS+.
source: Post hoc tests revealed that in both models, effects were driven by significantly lower SCRs to the CS+ (specificity model: F(1, 1400)=6.13, p=0.013, R2=0.004, dimensional model: ß=–0.004, t(1398)=–1.97, p=0.049, r=–0.07).
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical test results.

claim: Multicollinearity was not a concern in the dimensional model analyses based on variance inflation factor (VIF) values.
source: If we apply the rule of thumb of a variance inflation factor (VIF) >10, which is often used in the literature to indicate concerning multicollinearity (e.g. Hair et al., 1995; Mason et al., 1989; Neter et al., 1989), we can assume that multicollinearity was not a concern in our study (abuse: VIF=8.64; neglect: VIF=7.93).
evidence: The claim is based on VIF values calculated from the data and comparison to published thresholds.

claim: Greater exposure to neglect significantly predicted a generally lower SCR reactivity in the specificity model.
source: Furthermore, the statistical analyses of the specificity model additionally revealed that greater exposure to neglect significantly predicted a generally lower SCR reactivity (F(1, 1400)=4.3, p=0.038, R2=0.003)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from regression analyses.

claim: Greater exposure to neglect significantly predicted lower CS discrimination in contingency ratings during both acquisition training and the generalization test in the specificity model.
source: as well as a lower CS discrimination in contingency ratings during both acquisition training (F(1, 1400)=5.58, p=0.018, R2=0.004) and the generalization test (F(1, 1400)=6.33, p=0.012, R2=0.005; see Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from regression analyses.

claim: The effects of neglect on CS discrimination in contingency ratings were driven by significantly higher CS- responding in individuals exposed to neglect.
source: These were driven by significantly higher CS- responding in contingency ratings (acquisition training: F(1, 1400)=4.62, p=0.032, R2=0.003; generalization test: F(1, 1400)=8.38, p=0.004, R2=0.006) in individuals exposed to neglect.
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc statistical test results.

claim: None of the effect sizes from the exploratory analyses fell outside the confidence intervals of the main results for CS discrimination in SCRs during acquisition training.
source: None of the effect sizes from the exploratory analyses (cumulative risk, severity groups: d=0.14; cumulative risk, number of subscales exceeding an at least moderate cut-off: d=0.20; specificity model, abuse: d=0.10; specificity model, neglect: d=0.19; dimensional model: d=0.18) fell outside the confidence intervals of our main results (i.e. an at least moderate childhood adversity exposure: [0.03; 0.33]).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of effect sizes from different analyses.

claim: No evidence of differential explanatory strengths among theories was found.
source: Hence, we found no evidence of differential explanatory strengths among theories.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of effect sizes.

claim: Participants exposed to childhood adversity reported significantly higher trait anxiety and depression levels than unexposed participants.
source: As expected, participants exposed to childhood adversity reported significantly higher trait anxiety and depression levels than unexposed participants (all p's<0.001; see Table 3 and Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results presented in Table 3 and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The pattern of higher trait anxiety and depression in exposed individuals remained unchanged when childhood adversity was operationalized differently following the cumulative risk approach, the specificity, and the dimensional model.
source: This pattern remained unchanged when childhood adversity was operationalized differently - following the cumulative risk approach, the specificity, and the dimensional model (see the Materials and methods section). These additional analyses all indicated a significant positive relationship between exposure to childhood adversity and trait anxiety as well as depression scores irrespective of the specific operationalization of 'exposure' (see Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results from additional analyses reported in the Appendix.

claim: CS discrimination during acquisition training and the generalization phase, generalization gradients, and general reactivity in SCRs were unrelated to trait anxiety and depression scores with the exception of a significant association between depression scores and CS discrimination during fear acquisition training.
source: CS discrimination during acquisition training and the generalization phase, generalization gradients, and general reactivity in SCRs were unrelated to trait anxiety and depression scores in this sample with the exception of a significant association between depression scores and CS discrimination during fear acquisition training (see Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results reported in Appendix 1—table 8.

claim: A very small but significant negative correlation was observed indicating that high levels of depression were associated with reduced levels of CS discrimination during fear acquisition training.
source: More precisely, a very small but significant negative correlation was observed indicating that high levels of depression were associated with reduced levels of CS discrimination (r=–0.057, p=0.033).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis results.

claim: The correlation between trait anxiety levels and CS discrimination during fear acquisition training was not statistically significant.
source: The correlation between trait anxiety levels and CS discrimination during fear acquisition training was not statistically significant but on a descriptive level, high trait anxiety scores were also linked to lower CS discrimination scores (r=–0.05, p=0.06)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis results showing a non-significant relationship.

claim: The correlations between CS discrimination during fear acquisition training and trait anxiety and depression did not statistically differ from each other.
source: However, both correlations (i.e. CS discrimination during fear acquisition training and trait anxiety as well as depression, respectively) did not statistically differ from each other (z=0.303, p=0.762, Dunn and Clark, 1969).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results comparing correlations.

claim: Trait anxiety and depression scores were significantly associated with SCRs to the CS+, but not to the CS- during acquisition training.
source: Interestingly, and consistent with our results showing that the relationship between childhood adversity and CS discrimination was mainly driven by significantly lower CS+ responses in exposed individuals, trait anxiety and depression scores were significantly associated with SCRs to the CS+, but not to the CS- during acquisition training (see Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical results reported in Appendix 1—table 8.

claim: Individuals exposed to childhood adversity exhibited reduced CS discrimination in SCRs during both acquisition training and the generalization phase compared to those classified as unexposed.
source: In line with the conclusion of a recent systematic literature review (Ruge et al., 2024), individuals exposed to (an at least moderate level of) childhood adversity exhibited reduced CS discrimination in SCRs during both acquisition training and the generalization phase compared to those classified as unexposed (i.e. no or low exposure).
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study and is supported by the data presented.

claim: Generalization gradients were comparable between exposed and unexposed individuals.
source: Generalization gradients themselves were, however, comparable between exposed and unexposed individuals.
evidence: The claim summarizes a finding from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: The pattern of decreased CS discrimination driven primarily by reduced CS+ responding was observed despite substantial heterogeneity in childhood adversity assessment and operationalization, and despite differences in the experimental paradigms.
source: The systematic literature search by Ruge et al., 2024 revealed that the pattern of decreased CS discrimination, driven primarily by reduced CS+ responding, was observed despite substantial heterogeneity in childhood adversity assessment and operationalization, and despite differences in the experimental paradigms.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a systematic literature review by Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: The response pattern of individuals exposed to childhood adversity (reduced responding to the CS+) is remarkably different from what is typically observed in patients (enhanced responding to the CS-).
source: Although both individuals without mental disorders exposed to childhood adversity and patients suffering from anxiety- and stress-related disorders (e.g. Duits et al., 2015) show reduced CS discrimination, it is striking that the response pattern of individuals exposed to childhood adversity (i.e. reduced responding to the CS+) is remarkably different from what is typically observed in patients (i.e. enhanced responding to the CS-).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of findings from the current study with meta-analytic evidence from patient samples.

claim: Reduced CS discrimination driven by decreased CS+ responding may represent a resilience rather than a risk factor in individuals exposed to childhood adversity who remain mentally healthy.
source: Hence, it may be an obvious explanation that reduced CS discrimination driven by decreased CS+ responding may represent a resilience rather than a risk factor because individuals exposed to childhood adversity in our sample are mentally healthy despite being exposed to a strong risk factor.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the pattern of results.

claim: There is substantial heterogeneity in individual trajectories and profiles in the aftermath of childhood adversity exposures in humans and rodents.
source: In fact, there is substantial heterogeneity in individual trajectories and profiles in the aftermath of such exposures in humans and rodents (Russo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2012.

claim: While some individuals remain resilient despite exposure to childhood adversity, others develop psychopathological conditions.
source: While some individuals remain resilient despite exposure, others develop psychopathological conditions (Galea et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galea et al., 2005.

claim: The sample of the present study may represent a specific subsample of exposed individuals who are developing along a resilient trajectory.
source: Consequently, the sample of the present study may represent a specific subsample of exposed individuals who are developing along a resilient trajectory.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the characteristics of the sample.

claim: Reduced physiological reactivity to a signal of threat (CS+) may protect the individual from overwhelming physiological and/or emotional responses to potentially recurrent threats.
source: Thus, it can be speculated that reduced physiological reactivity to a signal of threat (e.g. CS+) may protect the individual from overwhelming physiological and/or emotional responses to potentially recurrent threats (for a discussion, see Ruge et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is explicitly speculative and based on inference, with reference to a discussion in Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: Decreased CS discrimination driven by reduced CS+ responding is observed rather consistently irrespective of whether the investigated samples were healthy, at risk, or included patients.
source: While this seems a plausible theoretical explanation, decreased CS discrimination driven by reduced CS+ responding is observed rather consistently and most importantly irrespective of whether the investigated samples were healthy, at risk, or included patients (Ruge et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruge et al., 2024.

claim: The response pattern of reduced CS+ responding might be a specific characteristic of childhood adversity exposure distinct from the response pattern generally observed in patients suffering from anxiety- and stress-related disorders.
source: Thus, this response pattern which was also observed in our study might be a specific characteristic of childhood adversity exposure distinct from the response pattern generally observed in patients suffering from anxiety- and stress-related disorders (i.e. increased responding to the CS-)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of results across studies.

claim: Individuals exposed to childhood adversity in this sample showed significantly higher anxiety and depression despite being free of any categorical diagnoses.
source: even though individuals exposed to childhood adversity in this sample indeed showed significantly higher anxiety and depression despite being free of any categorical diagnoses (see Appendix 1) which was also previously reported by e.g., Spinhoven et al., 2011 and Kuhn et al., 2016.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to previous reports.

claim: Trait anxiety and depression scores may be mediated by childhood adversity in their relationship with fear conditioning measures.
source: Although reported associations in the literature are heterogeneous (Lonsdorf et al., 2017), we may speculate that they may be mediated by childhood adversity. We conducted additional mediation analyses (data not shown) which, however, did not support this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is speculative and was tested but not supported by mediation analyses.

claim: Reduced skin conductance in children exposed to childhood adversity was observed during other tasks such as attention regulation during interpersonal conflict.
source: Yet, it is noteworthy that reduced skin conductance in children exposed to childhood adversity was also observed during other tasks such as attention regulation during interpersonal conflict (Pollak et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pollak et al., 2005.

claim: Reduced skin conductance in children exposed to childhood adversity was observed during passively viewing slides with emotional or cognitive content.
source: or passively viewing slides with emotional or cognitive content (Carrey et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carrey et al., 1995.

claim: Some studies did not find an association between childhood adversity and skin conductance.
source: whereas other studies did not find such an association (Ben-Amitay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ben-Amitay et al., 2016.

claim: In various threat-related studies, enhanced responding or no significant differences in skin conductance were observed across outcome measures in individuals exposed to childhood adversity.
source: Moreover, in various threat-related studies, also enhanced responding or no significant differences were observed across outcome measures (Estrada et al., 2020; Huskey et al., 2022; Jovanovic et al., 2009; Jovanovic et al., 2022; Kreutzer and Gorka, 2021; Lis et al., 2020; Pole et al., 2007; Rowland et al., 2022; Thome et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Differences in general reactivity need to be taken into account for data analyses and interpretation.
source: While generally blunted responding might be particularly related to decreased CS+ responding in the present study, differences in general reactivity need to be taken into account for data analyses and interpretation
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: The exclusion of physiological non-responders or 'non-learners' has been common in the field until recently.
source: in particular as the exclusion of physiological non-responders or so-called 'non-learners' (i.e. individuals not showing a minimum discrimination score between SCRs to the CS+ and CS-) has been common in the field until recently (for a critical discussion, see Lonsdorf et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lonsdorf et al., 2019 discussing this practice.

claim: In a subsample of this study, fear generalization phenotypes explained less variance compared to CS discrimination and general reactivity.
source: In a subsample of this study, it was previously observed that fear generalization phenotypes explained less variance as compared to CS discrimination and general reactivity (Stegmann et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication using a subsample of the current study.

claim: CS discrimination and general reactivity but not fear generalization predicted increases in anxiety and depression scores during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: and CS discrimination as well as general reactivity but not fear generalization predicted increases in anxiety and depression scores during the COVID-19 pandemic (Imholze et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Imholze et al., 2023.

claim: The lack of associations with fear generalization measures may be specific to the paradigm and sample used in these studies.
source: The lack of associations with fear generalization measures (i.e. LDS) may be specific to the paradigm and sample used in these studies, but it may also be an interesting lead for future work to disentangle the relationship between CS discrimination, general reactivity, and generalization gradients, as they have been suggested to be interrelated (Imholze et al., 2023; Stegmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the findings, with citations to related work.

claim: The current results converge with the literature in identifying reduced CS discrimination and decreased CS+ responding as key characteristics in individuals exposed to childhood adversity.
source: In sum, the current results converge with the literature in identifying reduced CS discrimination and decreased CS+ responding as key characteristics in individuals exposed to childhood adversity.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding and its consistency with the literature.

claim: The various operationalizations of childhood adversity represent a challenge for integrating the current results into the existing literature.
source: As highlighted recently (see Koppold et al., 2023; Ruge et al., 2024), the various operationalizations of childhood adversity as well as general trauma (Karstoft and Armour, 2023) represent a challenge for integrating the current results into the existing literature.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent publications discussing this challenge.

claim: The translation of verbal theories about childhood adversity into precise statistical tests proved to be a challenging task paved by operationalizational ambiguity.
source: First, the translation of these verbal theories into precise statistical tests proved to be a rather challenging task paved by operationalizational ambiguity.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experience in conducting the exploratory analyses.

claim: Current verbal theories about childhood adversity are, at least to a certain degree, ill-defined.
source: We have collected some key challenges in Table 1 and conclude that current verbal theories are, at least to a certain degree, ill-defined, as our attempt has disclosed a multiverse of different, equally plausible ways to test them - even though we provide only a limited number of exemplary tests.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the challenges encountered in translating theories into statistical tests.

claim: Despite challenges in operationalization, the results of most tests converged in identifying an effect of childhood adversity on reduced CS discrimination in SCRs during acquisition training.
source: Second, despite these challenges, the results of most tests converged in identifying an effect of childhood adversity on reduced CS discrimination in SCRs during acquisition training, which is reassuring when aiming to integrate results based on different operationalizations.
evidence: The claim is based on the convergence of results across different operationalizations in the exploratory analyses.

claim: None of the theories tested appears to be explanatorily superior.
source: Third, none of the theories appears to be explanatorily superior.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of effect sizes across different theoretical operationalizations.

claim: The results are not in line with predictions of the dimensional model which posits a specific association between exposure to threat- but not deprivation-related childhood adversity and fear conditioning performance.
source: Fourth, our results are not in line with predictions of the dimensional model (Machlin et al., 2019; McLaughlin et al., 2021) which posits a specific association between exposure to threat- but not deprivation-related childhood adversity and fear conditioning performance. If anything, our results point in the opposite direction.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the study results with theoretical predictions of the dimensional model.

claim: Neither considering childhood adversity as a broad category, nor different subtypes have consistently shown to strongly map onto biological mechanisms.
source: Taken together, neither considering childhood adversity as a broad category, nor different subtypes have consistently shown to strongly map onto biological mechanisms (for an in-depth discussion, see Smith and Pollak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith and Pollak, 2021.

claim: There is an urgent need for additional exploration, refinement, and testing of current theories linking childhood adversity to psychopathology.
source: Hence, even though it is currently the dominant view in the field, that considering the potentially distinct effects of dissociable adversity types holds promise to provide mechanistic insights into how childhood adversity becomes biologically embedded (Berens et al., 2017; Kuhlman et al., 2017; Smith and Pollak, 2021), we emphasize the urgent need for additional exploration, refinement, and testing of current theories.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the findings and their implications for theory development.

claim: Effect sizes of associations between exposure to childhood adversity and fear conditioning performance were small despite being significant in a large sample.
source: First, despite our observation of significant associations between exposure to childhood adversity and fear conditioning performance in a large sample, it should be noted that effect sizes were small.
evidence: The claim is based on the effect sizes reported in the study results.

claim: The study cannot provide a comparison of potential group differences in unconditioned responding to the US.
source: Second, we cannot provide a comparison of potential group differences in unconditioned responding to the US. This is, however, important as this comparison may explain group differences in conditioned responding - a mechanism that remains unexplored to date (Ruge et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the study design.

claim: The CTQ focuses exclusively on the presence or absence of exposure without consideration of individual and exposure characteristics that have been shown to be of crucial relevance.
source: Third, the use of the CTQ, which is the most commonly used questionnaire in the field (see Ruge et al., 2024), comes with a number of disadvantages. Most prominently, the CTQ focuses exclusively on the presence or absence of exposure without consideration of individual and exposure characteristics that have been shown to be of crucial relevance (Danese and Widom, 2023; see Smith and Pollak, 2021), such as controllability, burdening, exposure severity, duration, and developmental timing.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the CTQ assessment tool, supported by citations.

claim: Testing the topological approach requires an extremely large dataset including in-depth phenotyping, which was not available in this study.
source: These characteristics are embedded in the framework of the topological approach (Smith and Pollak, 2021), another important model linking childhood adversity exposure to negative outcomes, which, however, was not evaluated in the present work. Testing this model requires an extremely large dataset including in-depth phenotyping, which was not available here, but may be an important avenue for future work.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the current study and suggests future directions.

claim: Significant effects of childhood adversity have been shown primarily on physiological reactivity (SCR) across all theories tested.
source: Fourth, across all theories, significant effects of childhood adversity have been shown primarily on physiological reactivity (i.e. SCR).
evidence: The claim summarizes a pattern observed across the different analyses in the study.

claim: Whether the findings are specific to SCRs or might generalize to other physiological outcome measures remains an open question for future studies.
source: Whether these findings are specific to SCRs or might generalize to other physiological outcome measures such as fear-potentiated startle, heart rate, or local changes in neural activation, remains an open question for future studies.
evidence: The claim identifies a limitation and suggests future research directions.

claim: The ability to distinguish threat from safety is key to an individual's ability to dynamically adapt to changing environmental demands.
source: In sum, when ultimately aiming to understand the impact of exposure to adversity on the development of psychopathological symptoms (Anda et al., 2006; Felitti, 2002; Gilbert et al., 2009; Green et al., 2010; Heim and Nemeroff, 2001; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Moffitt et al., 2007; Teicher et al., 2022), it is crucial to understand the biological mechanisms through which exposure to adversity 'gets under the skin.' To achieve this, emotional-associative learning can serve as a prime translational model for fear and anxiety disorders: One plausible mechanism is the ability to distinguish threat from safety, which is key to an individual's ability to dynamically adapt to changing environmental demands (Craske et al., 2012; Vervliet et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Craske et al., 2012 and Vervliet et al., 2013.

claim: The ability to distinguish threat from safety appears to be impaired in individuals with a history of childhood adversity.
source: - an ability that appears to be impaired in individuals with a history of childhood adversity.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of the study.

claim: The identification of risk and resilience factors following exposure to childhood adversity is essential for the development of effective intervention and prevention programs.
source: This mechanism is of particular relevance to the development of stress- and anxiety-related psychopathology, as the identification of risk but also resilience factors following exposure to childhood adversity is essential for the development of effective intervention and prevention programs.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the practical implications of the research.

claim: 1678 healthy participants were recruited in a multi-centric study at the Universities of Münster, Würzburg, and Hamburg, Germany.
source: In total, 1678 healthy participants (ageM=25.26 years, ageSD=5.58 years, female=60.10%, male=39.30%) were recruited in a multi-centric study at the Universities of Münster, Würzburg, and Hamburg, Germany (SFB TRR58).
evidence: The claim describes the study sample and is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Data from parts of the Würzburg sample have been reported previously.
source: Data from parts of the Würzburg sample have been reported previously (Herzog et al., 2021; Imholze et al., 2023; Schiele et al., 2020; Schiele et al., 2016a; Schiele et al., 2016b; Stegmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Previous reports using parts of this sample addressed research questions different from the ones investigated in the current study.
source: These previous reports, also those focusing on experimental fear conditioning (Schiele et al., 2016a; Stegmann et al., 2019), addressed, however, research questions different from the ones investigated here (see also Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: The claim clarifies the novelty of the current study relative to previous publications.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committees of the three Universities.
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committees of the three Universities (Münster: 2016–131-b-S, Ethics Committee Westfalen-Lippe; Würzburg: Votum 07/08, Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the University of Würzburg; Hamburg: PV2755, Ethics Committee of the General Medical Council Hamburg)
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about ethical approval.

claim: The study was conducted in agreement with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: and was conducted in agreement with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about ethical conduct.

claim: Current and/or lifetime diagnosis of DSM-IV mental Axis-I disorders led to exclusion from the study.
source: Current and/or lifetime diagnosis of DSM-IV mental Axis-I disorders, as assessed by the German version of the Mini International Psychiatric Interview (Sheehan et al., 1998), led to exclusion from the study
evidence: The claim describes an exclusion criterion for the study.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent and received 50 € as compensation.
source: All participants provided written informed consent and received 50 € as compensation.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about study procedures.

claim: 276 participants were excluded from the statistical analyses due to missing data, technical reasons, and deviating from the study protocol.
source: A reduced number of 1402 participants (ageM=25.38 years, ageSD=5.76 years, female=60.30%, male=39.70%) were included in the statistical analyses because 276 participants were excluded due to missing data (CTQ: n=21, ratings: n=78, SCRs: n=182), for technical reasons, and due to deviating from the study protocol.
evidence: The claim describes the final sample size and reasons for exclusions.

claim: Physiological SCR non-responders or non-learners were not excluded from the analyses.
source: We did not exclude physiological SCR non-responders or non-learners, as this procedure has been shown to induce bias through predominantly excluding specific subpopulations (e.g. high trait anxiety), which may be particularly prevalent in individuals exposed to childhood adversity (Lonsdorf et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological decision with justification based on a citation.

claim: Participants underwent a fear conditioning and generalization paradigm which was adapted from Lau et al., 2008.
source: Participants underwent a fear conditioning and generalization paradigm which was adapted from Lau et al., 2008 and described previously in detail (Herzog et al., 2021; Schiele et al., 2016a; Stegmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental paradigm with citations to the original and previous descriptions.

claim: Participants provided ratings of the faces with regards to valence, arousal, and US contingencies at the end of each experimental phase and after half of the total acquisition and generalization trials.
source: At the end of each experimental phase (habituation, acquisition training, and generalization) as well as after half of the total acquisition and generalization trials, participants provided ratings of the faces with regards to valence, arousal (9-point Likert-scales; from 1=very unpleasant/very calm to 9=very pleasant/very arousing) and US contingencies (11-point Likert-scale; from 0 to 100% in 10% increments).
evidence: The claim describes the rating procedure used in the study.

claim: Skin conductance was recorded continuously using Brainproducts V-Amp-16 and Vision Recorder software at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz from the non-dominant hand.
source: Skin conductance was recorded continuously using Brainproducts V-Amp-16 and Vision Recorder software (Brainproducts, Gilching, Germany) at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz from the non-dominant hand (thenar and hypothenar eminences) using two Ag/AgCl electrodes.
evidence: The claim describes the physiological data recording procedure.

claim: Data were analyzed offline using BrainVision Analyzer 2 software.
source: Data were analyzed offline using BrainVision Analyzer 2 software (Brainproducts, Gilching, Germany).
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis software used.

claim: The signal was filtered offline with a high cut-off filter of 1 Hz and a notch filter of 50 Hz.
source: The signal was filtered offline with a high cut-off filter of 1 Hz and a notch filter of 50 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the signal processing procedure.

claim: Amplitudes of SCRs were quantified by using the Trough-to-peak (TTP) approach.
source: Amplitudes of SCRs were quantified by using the Trough-to-peak (TTP) approach.
evidence: The claim describes the method for quantifying SCRs.

claim: The response onset was defined as between 900–4000 ms after stimulus onset and the peak between 2000–6000 ms after stimulus onset according to published guidelines.
source: According to published guidelines (Boucsein et al., 2012), the response onset was defined as between 900–4000 ms after stimulus onset and the peak between 2000–6000 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: The claim describes the SCR scoring procedure with citation to published guidelines.

claim: A minimum response criterion of 0.02 μS was applied, with lower individual responses scored as zero.
source: A minimum response criterion of 0.02 μS was applied, with lower individual responses scored as zero (i.e. non-responses).
evidence: The claim describes the minimum response criterion used in SCR scoring.

claim: Log-transformation and range-correction were used for SCR data because these transformations are standard practice in the authors' laboratory and approximate a normal distribution more closely.
source: We used log-transformation and range-correction for SCR data because these transformations are standard practice in our laboratory and we strive for methodological consistency across different projects (e.g. Ehlers et al., 2020; Kuhn et al., 2016; Scharfenort et al., 2016; Sjouwerman and Lonsdorf, 2020; Sjouwerman et al., 2015). Additionally, log-transformed and range-corrected data are generally assumed to approximate a normal distribution more closely and exhibit lower error variance, which leads to larger effect sizes (Lykken, 1972; Lykken and Venables, 1971; Sjouwerman et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim describes and justifies the data transformation approach with citations.

claim: Log-transformed and range-corrected SCR data appear to offer greater reliability compared to using raw data alone on a descriptive level.
source: Additionally, on a descriptive level, this combination of transformations appears to offer greater reliability compared to using raw data alone (Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klingelhöfer-Jens et al., 2022.

claim: Participants completed a computerized battery of questionnaires prior to the experiment.
source: Participants completed a computerized battery of questionnaires (for a full list, see Stegmann et al., 2019) prior to the experiment
evidence: The claim describes the psychometric assessment procedure.

claim: The CTQ contains 28 items for the retrospective assessment of childhood adversity across five subscales and a control scale.
source: The CTQ contains 28 items for the retrospective assessment of childhood adversity across five subscales (emotional, physical, and sexual abuse, as well as emotional and physical neglect; for internal consistency, see Appendix 1), and a control scale.
evidence: The claim describes the structure of the CTQ assessment tool.

claim: The STAI-T consists of 20 items addressing trait anxiety.
source: The STAI-T consists of 20 items addressing trait anxiety (Laux and Spielberger, 1981; Spielberger, 1983)
evidence: The claim describes the STAI-T assessment tool with citations.

claim: The ADS-K includes 15 items assessing depressiveness during the past 7 days.
source: and the ADS-K includes 15 items assessing depressiveness during the past 7 d.
evidence: The claim describes the ADS-K assessment tool.

claim: CS discrimination was calculated by separately averaging responses to CS+ and CS- across trials and subtracting averaged CS- responses from averaged CS+ responses.
source: CS discrimination was calculated by separately averaging responses to CS+ and CS- across trials (except the first acquisition trial) and subtracting averaged CS- responses from averaged CS+ responses.
evidence: The claim describes the calculation method for CS discrimination.

claim: The first acquisition trial was excluded from CS discrimination calculation as no learning could possibly have taken place due to the delay conditioning paradigm.
source: The first acquisition trial was excluded as no learning could possibly have taken place due to the delay conditioning paradigm.
evidence: The claim explains the rationale for excluding the first trial from analysis.

claim: The LDS was calculated by subtracting the mean responses to all GSs from the mean responses to both CSs during the generalization phase.
source: The LDS was calculated by subtracting the mean responses to all GSs from the mean responses to both CSs during the generalization phase.
evidence: The claim describes the calculation method for the LDS.

claim: General reactivity in SCRs and ratings was calculated by averaging trials across all stimuli and phases.
source: To calculate the general reactivity in SCRs and ratings, trials were averaged across all stimuli (CSs and GSs) and phases (i.e. habituation, acquisition training, and generalization phase).
evidence: The claim describes the calculation method for general reactivity.

claim: Raw SCRs were used for analyses of general physiological reactivity.
source: Note that raw SCRs were used for analyses of general physiological reactivity.
evidence: The claim describes a specific methodological choice in data analysis.

claim: CS discrimination during acquisition training and the generalization phase, LDS, and general reactivity were compared between participants who were exposed and unexposed to childhood adversity by using two-tailed independent-samples t-tests.
source: CS discrimination during acquisition training and the generalization phase, LDS, and general reactivity were compared between participants who were exposed and unexposed to childhood adversity by using two-tailed independent-samples t-tests.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: A two-way mixed ANOVA was conducted to examine the effect of childhood adversity exposure on responses to the CS+ and CS-.
source: For CS discrimination in SCRs, a two-way mixed ANOVA was conducted to examine the effect of childhood adversity exposure on responses to the CS+ and CS- by including CS type and childhood adversity exposure as independent variables.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical analysis approach for examining CS type effects.

claim: No correction for alpha inflation was applied in the exploratory analyses, given their exploratory nature.
source: Note that no correction for alpha inflation was applied in these analyses, given their exploratory nature.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological decision in the exploratory analyses.
